name: PT Arthavest Tbk

frontmatter.title: Arthavest: one hotel, a fixed cost base, and a price with no fundamental anchor
frontmatter.summary: Arthavest owns a single hotel in Central Jakarta through a majority-owned subsidiary and almost nothing else. Revenue fell a third in 2025 and again in the first half of 2026 while the cost base did not move, leaving the group loss-making and the hotel barely EBITDA-positive. On our numbers the equity is worth a fraction of the market price. SELL, target Rp199.
thesis: The price is not an estimate of value: at the last traded price the market capitalisation is more than a dozen times a full year of revenue and over a hundred times last-twelve-month EBITDA for a single hotel.

Revenue has fallen for two consecutive periods while costs have not: FY2025 revenue dropped a third to IDR71.4bn and the first half of 2026 fell again to IDR26.4bn, but operating expenses were IDR28.6bn in the half, above IDR27.0bn a year earlier.

The company's own plan is not an anchor: it targeted IDR100.0bn of revenue for 2025 and delivered 71.4% of it, then set the same target for 2026 while running at a rate that implies about two-thirds of that.

Capital allocation changed direction: IDR37.0bn of the group's cash went into a stake in an unrelated listed property developer in H1 2026, taking cash down to IDR8.6bn and cutting the interest income that had been propping up the P&L.
Our two methods bracket value between Rp195 a share on the cash flows and Rp337 on a hotel-peer book multiple; even the more generous of them is a fraction of the market price.

catalysts.event: FY2026 results - first full-year test of whether the revenue target was abandoned or missed again
Audited FY2026 accounts: mark-to-market on the listed-securities portfolio and any impairment of the hotel's fixed assets
AGM - dividend decision after a second loss-making year

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp199 a share against a last price of Rp2,110, an expected return of -90.6%. The target is restated from the previous publication: the minority interest is now deducted at its look-through value rather than at its book value, which lifts the DCF value of the equity from the low fifties a share to Rp195 and the target to Rp199. The rating does not change — the shares still trade a multiple of anything the hotel's cash flows support — but the earlier expected return of about minus ninety-five per cent was too harsh, and it is corrected here.** The target is the probability-weighted output of the three scenario valuations, cut by a 20.0% liquidity discount because the shares turn over IDR188.8m a day, the tier in fund rules that fixes the haircut off traded value; it is a tradability charge, not a view of the business, and it is charged once, here, and never again as a premium inside the discount rate. The DCF and the P/BV cross-check disagree — that disagreement is the point of this report, and we explain it in the valuation section rather than hiding it in an average.

Arthavest is a holding company whose only operating asset is the REDTOP Hotel & Convention Center, 390 rooms on Jalan Pecenongan in Central Jakarta, held through a 51.0% stake in PT Sanggraha Dhika [S2]. The remaining 49.0% sits with non-controlling interests whose book value is IDR101.6bn [S3]. There is no second business, no development pipeline, and no land bank beyond the hotel site. The company describes itself as an investment firm; in practice it is a single-asset hotel owner with a small securities portfolio bolted on.

The variant view is not subtle. The market is paying a market capitalisation of IDR942.5bn for a business that generated IDR71.4bn of revenue and IDR8.3bn of EBITDA in FY2025, and which reported an operating loss, EBITDA of IDR8.3bn falling short of depreciation of IDR15.1bn [S0][S2]. Our base case has revenue of IDR66.5bn in 2026 — below the reported 2025 level — because the first half actually came in at IDR26.4bn against IDR28.4bn a year earlier, and the second half would need to be nearly three times the first to reach the company's target [S3].

What moves the value is therefore not growth but the cost line and the securities portfolio. The hotel's cash operating cost base has barely moved in nominal terms across a revenue swing of more than a quarter, so every rupiah of revenue recovery falls almost entirely to EBITDA; that is the bull case, and it is real. Against it, the group converted IDR37.0bn of cash into listed equities in the first half of 2026 — a stake in PT Intiland Development Tbk — which both removes the interest income that flattered 2025 and puts the parent's liquidity at the mercy of a share price it does not control [S3].

Three facts carry the call. First, the price. The shares trade at a valuation no operating metric supports: IDR71.4bn of revenue against a market capitalisation of IDR942.5bn, with 390 rooms. Second, the cost structure. A hotel running at 38.0% occupancy against a Jakarta market at 60.0% in December 2025 and 58.2% in September 2026 has to close a large demand gap before the fixed base stops eating the gross profit [S2][S5]. Third, the ownership. 84.2% of the shares are held by one controlling shareholder, so the price is set by a thin float and is not evidence about value [S2].

We would be wrong if the hotel's occupancy recovered to the market average quickly and the group sold the securities at a premium — the bull case, worth Rp319 a share on our own model, still leaves the shares far below the current price. The bear case is worth Rp186. There is no scenario in our model, and none we can construct from the filings, that supports the market price.
What the company owns

PT Arthavest Tbk listed in 2002 as PT Artha Securities Tbk and changed its name in 2005; it began as an investment holding company and only entered hospitality when it bought 51.0% of PT Sanggraha Dhika, the owner and operator of the REDTOP Hotel & Convention Center [S2]. The Articles of Association still describe the business as "other management consultation activities", which tells you how little the legal shell has to do with the economics.

The hotel is a four-star business property with 390 rooms across three categories — superior, deluxe and suites — plus a convention and banquet facility, meeting rooms, a business centre, restaurant and bar, swimming pool, fitness centre and spa [S2]. It sits in the Pecenongan area of Central Jakarta, within reach of the State Palace and government offices, the Glodok and Mangga Dua commercial districts, and a short drive from Soekarno-Hatta airport [S2]. That location explains both the historical customer mix — government, institutional and corporate MICE — and the vulnerability: when the government cuts travel and meeting budgets, this hotel feels it first.
Revenue mix

The P&L is split into five revenue departments, and the mix has shifted with the demand shock. In FY2025 rooms produced the largest share of revenue and food and beverage most of the rest, with fitness and spa, laundry and other services making up the balance [S2]. Two years earlier the same hotel sold more room nights at a higher average rate; in FY2025 it sold 52,956 room nights at an average rate of Rp725,329, having run at 46.2% occupancy in FY2024 before the fall to 38.0% [S2].

The operating leverage is extreme and is the single most important fact in this report. Cost of revenue is only about a third of sales because a hotel's departmental costs — food cost, laundry, spa supplies — scale with covers. Everything else does not. Operating expenses were IDR54.7bn in FY2025 against IDR58.6bn in FY2024 on revenue that fell by a third, and general and administrative expenses were the overwhelming majority of that [S2]. Strip out depreciation and the cash cost base has barely moved in nominal terms, and it is mostly payroll for the group's 155 employees [S2]. A hotel with this cost structure is a bet on occupancy, and occupancy has gone the wrong way.
Strategy and the company's own plan

Management's stated response to the 2025 shock was to pivot from public-sector to private corporate demand, to push "MICE hybrid" — meetings with streaming for remote participants — and to upgrade several meeting rooms [S2][S4]. In the 2026 public expose the company set a revenue target of IDR100.0bn [S2][S4]. We treat that target as aspiration rather than forecast, for a documented reason: the 2025 target was the same figure and the company delivered 71.4% of it [S2]. A plan that has missed by nearly a third once and is being repeated unchanged while the first half runs below the prior year is not a basis for estimates.
Competitive position

REDTOP competes in a Jakarta four-star market that added supply through the last decade and is now fighting for a demand pool that shrank when the government tightened spending. The hotel has no brand affiliation with an international operator, no loyalty programme of scale, and no management contract with a global chain; its advantages are location, a large convention floor, and a very low cost of capital (no debt). Its disadvantage is that the physical plant is old, which is why depreciation is IDR15.1bn a year on net book value of IDR191.6bn and why the 2025 capex programme included a one-off furniture and equipment renewal [S2].

We would characterise it as a challenger with a location moat that is thinning: the site cannot be replicated, but the building can be out-competed on product [S2]. In the five-forces frame, supplier power is low, buyer power is high (corporate and government clients tender), the threat of substitutes is high (new supply plus alternative meeting formats), and rivalry is intense. That is a structure in which a single independent hotel earns its cost of capital only at high occupancy — which is precisely what the numbers show [S2].
The Jakarta hotel cycle

Jakarta's star-rated hotel occupancy is the cleanest single indicator for this company, and it has been unusually volatile. In 2025 it ran from the high thirties in March to the high fifties by October and above sixty per cent in November before closing the year at 60.0% [S2]. In September 2026 BPS DKI put the city's occupancy at 58.2%, so the market has held most of its recovery even as this hotel's own occupancy sat near 38.0% [S5].

That gap — market occupancy near sixty per cent, REDTOP at 38.0% — is the core analytical problem. Either the hotel's product and location have lost share permanently, or there is a large recovery available as the corporate segment is rebuilt. Our base case takes the middle: occupancy improves from 38.0% toward the low forties, not back to the 46.2% of 2024, and average room rates grow with inflation rather than reverting [S2]. That produces revenue of IDR84.8bn by 2030 — still well below the IDR105.2bn peak.

The demand side has three components and they move differently. Government and state-enterprise meetings were the shock absorber that failed in 2025; corporate MICE and project teams are cyclical with the Jakarta construction and services economy; and leisure and transit demand is the smallest part of this hotel's mix but the most price-elastic. Because the convention floor is the fixed asset that drives the room base, the hotel's revenue is levered to the first two, and neither has a policy tailwind at present [S2].

BPS DKI data make the same point from the demand side. City-wide star-rated occupancy was 58.3% in July 2026, up both month on month and year on year, and foreign guests were choosing four-star hotels more than any other class (40.6% of foreign guest nights) [S6]. So the segment this hotel competes in is still being chosen by the customers it needs. That makes the occupancy gap a company problem before it is a market problem — which is the uncomfortable conclusion for management and, at a sensible price, the interesting one for a buyer.

Jakarta's hotel market is a classic cyclical oligopoly with a long supply pipeline: new four- and five-star rooms are commissioned years after the decision to build, so occupancy and rates overshoot in both directions. Independent single-asset hotels without a global distribution system typically trade at a discount to branded peers in both occupancy and rate, and they carry higher maintenance capex because the building ages without a chain's refurbishment cycle. In markets like this, the asset value of the land often exceeds the going-concern value of the hotel during a downturn — which is the situation we describe here.
Regulation and policy

The dominant external influence on this company is fiscal, not touristic. The annual report names Presidential Instruction No. 1 of 2025 — the government's budget-efficiency mandate across all state bodies — as the primary cause of the 2025 collapse, because it cut exactly the government meetings, training and travel that filled the convention floor [S2]. That is a policy shock with no scheduled end, and it is why we do not extrapolate a 2024-style recovery.

Two smaller regulatory items matter for the cost line and the accounts. The VAT regime changed in January 2025 under PMK 131/2024, which affects hotel and restaurant pricing mechanics [S2]. And the group's labour and severance obligations run through PSAK 24 provisions which, while small here, are a fixed claim ahead of shareholders.
Market share and the moat

We cannot measure market share directly — the company does not disclose Jakarta-wide room supply or its own share — but the ratio of its occupancy to the city's is a usable proxy: 38.0% against a market in the high fifties implies a share of demand well below its share of rooms, and that ratio deteriorated through 2025 [S2][S5]. The moat, such as it is, is the land and the convention floor. Brand, distribution and loyalty — the things that sustain hotel pricing power — are absent [S2]. We therefore do not give the hotel any terminal-value credit for a widening moat; the DCF fades returns rather than extending them (see the valuation section).
The five-year record

The history is a small, operationally geared business inside a debt-free balance sheet. Revenue went from IDR57.8bn in FY2022 to IDR77.7bn, then IDR105.2bn at the post-pandemic peak, then back to IDR71.4bn [S0][S2]. Gross margin held between 62.1% and 67.1% throughout, which confirms that the departmental cost line is genuinely variable and that the problem is not pricing but volume. The EBITDA line tells the story: IDR22.0bn in the good year, IDR8.3bn in the bad one, and an operating loss in FY2025 once depreciation of IDR15.1bn is charged [S0].

Below the operating line the accounts are unusual in two ways. First, interest income has been a material contributor — IDR2.7bn in FY2025 on a cash balance that peaked at IDR76.4bn — which is why a hotel with an operating loss still reported only a small net loss [S2]. Second, the split between the parent and the minority is wide: minorities took a positive share of the consolidated net loss, so the loss attributable to shareholders was larger than the group result, because the hotel subsidiary's result and the parent's own items moved in opposite directions [S2]. For forecasting we apply the 49.0% minority share consistently and disclose the simplification; the valuation bridge deducts the minority at its look-through value rather than at the IDR101.6bn book carrying amount, for the reason set out in the valuation section [S3].
Restating the depreciation charge

The data pack's depreciation for FY2024 is higher than the audited number, so we restate both years from the notes. The LK's property-and-equipment note shows depreciation of IDR15.3bn in 2024 and IDR15.1bn in 2025 [S2]. The pack's FY2024 figure overstates the non-cash add-back and would understate EBITDA in the base year. There is no corresponding distortion in 2025, where the two agree closely. We also confirm the group carries no borrowings and no remaining lease liabilities: the small 2024 lease obligation was settled, and 2025 lease payments were nil [S2]. The model carries total liabilities as its funding base and calibrates the effective finance cost to the LK's actual charge; the valuation bridge uses balance-sheet net cash and is unaffected.
The 2026 run-rate

The first half of 2026 is the most informative data point in the file, because it is the first period after the policy shock with a clean comparison. Revenue was IDR26.4bn against IDR28.4bn a year earlier, a fall in the high single digits; room revenue fell faster than food and beverage [S3]. Operating expenses were IDR28.6bn, above IDR27.0bn in the prior-year half, with general and administrative costs rising faster than staff costs [S3]. Put together, the operating loss widened and the reported loss attributable to shareholders was another loss [S3].

That is why our FY2026 revenue estimate is IDR66.5bn rather than the company's target. Applying the FY2025 seasonal pattern — the second half produced about half as much again as the first — to the IDR26.4bn first half gives about IDR66.5bn; reaching IDR100.0bn would require a second half nearly three times the first, which no evidence supports [S2][S3]. Forecast revenue growth is therefore -6.9% for 2026 and then a recovery in the mid single digits a year to IDR84.8bn in 2030.
Margins and costs

We hold gross margin at 67.0%, essentially the 67.1% achieved in FY2025 and the margin reported for the first half of 2026, because the departmental cost line scales with volume and there is no evidence of input-cost inflation that the hotel cannot pass through [S2][S3]. The operating expense ratio is where our forecast departs from history and where we expect the red team to push: we model opex at 84.7% of revenue in 2026, falling to 65.5% in 2030. That decline is not an efficiency assumption — it is what a fixed cost base of roughly IDR56.3bn looks like against rising revenue. Cash operating cost has been flat in nominal terms across the swing, so we grow it with inflation and let the ratio fall only because the denominator recovers [S2][S3].

EBITDA follows from those two lines: IDR3.6bn in 2026, rising to IDR15.8bn by 2030 — still below the IDR22.0bn of the 2024 peak. EBIT stays negative until 2030, because depreciation of IDR15.3bn a year consumes the EBITDA [S0]. This is a hotel that has to be much fuller than 38.0% before it earns an accounting profit.
Cash flow, capex and the balance sheet

Capex is the second swing factor. FY2025 capex was IDR11.0bn on the cash-flow statement, and the LK's own breakdown shows that IDR11.0bn of investment spending included a IDR7.6bn-scale one-off — specifically IDR7.6bn of hotel furniture and equipment renewal out of the IDR11.0bn total [S2 p.67]; FY2024 capex was IDR5.8bn. We model maintenance capex falling from IDR9.3bn to IDR10.1bn, below the depreciation charge, on the view that a building carried at IDR191.6bn net and depreciated over four to twenty years does not need replacement capex equal to its accounting charge every year [S2]. The key test is whether our assumption is aggressive or cautious: our modelled maintenance capex is well above the FY2024 actual of IDR5.8bn and above the non-recurring-stripped 2025 figure, so the assumption is not a disguised understatement of investment. The corollary cuts both ways: if capex were held at the FY2025 total in perpetuity, the DCF value would be lower than the number we publish; if it were held at the FY2024 level, the DCF would be higher.

Working capital is negative — the hotel collects at check-out and holds deposits — and we hold it at -6.0% of revenue [S0]. With EBITDA thin and capex above it, free cash flow is negative through 2028 and only turns positive in the terminal period; that is the arithmetic behind the DCF result in the valuation section.

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the company and the reason a zero value would be wrong. At 30 June 2026 the group had IDR144.3bn of equity attributable to shareholders, IDR101.6bn of minority interest, cash of IDR8.6bn and listed securities at fair value of IDR47.5bn [S3]. Fixed assets are carried at IDR191.6bn net, including land of IDR124.6bn at cost with no revaluation [S2]. The company is debt-free, which removes refinancing risk entirely and is why the bear case is a value problem rather than a solvency problem.
Earnings quality

Running the house screens: the accruals picture is unremarkable for a hotel — the gap between net profit and operating cash flow is explained by depreciation, and cash conversion is credible [S0]. Where the accounts deserve scrutiny is capital allocation, not accruals. In the first half of 2026 the group spent IDR37.0bn buying shares of PT Intiland Development Tbk, a listed property developer unrelated to the hotel, taking the securities portfolio to IDR47.5bn at fair value and cash down to IDR8.6bn [S3]. The purchase is disclosed as a plain FVOCI equity investment; the notes confirm there was no revenue from related parties in the period [S3]. Whatever its merits as an investment, it converted the group's liquidity into mark-to-market exposure to a cyclical developer at the moment the operating business needed a buffer, and it removed the interest income that had been supporting the P&L — interest income roughly halved year on year [S3].

There are no going-concern, negative-equity or late-filing notations in the record; the group is in special monitoring only in the sense that its shares are thinly traded [S2]. The controlling shareholder holds 84.2% and there are no pledged-share disclosures in the annual report [S2]. We treat the securities purchase as an optics-class governance flag rather than a manipulation-class one: it is disclosed, board-approved and priced daily, but it is not what a minority holder in a single-asset hotel would choose.
Why this method set

A single-asset hotel with visible cash flows is best valued on the cash flows those assets produce, cross-checked against what the assets would fetch. We therefore run a discounted cash flow as the primary method and a price-to-book (P/BV) on hotel peers as the asset cross-check. The industry card's default three-way split — DCF, EV/EBITDA and P/E — cannot be run here for reasons that are specific to this company: there is no positive trailing net profit to capitalise, so P/E is unavailable; and on the hotel peer set only two names print a usable EV/EBITDA multiple, which is below the engine's three-peer minimum, so an EV/EBITDA cross-check built on Jakarta hotels is not available rather than being borrowed from restaurants, golf courses and theme parks. Weights are 85% DCF and 15% book value, with the P/E weight moved to book because book is the only asset anchor this company has [S0]. A reader who prefers a pure DCF should note that it produces the lower of our two values.

The peer set is the Jakarta hotel and lodging names on the exchange — JIHD, PSKT, SHID, BUVA, PJAA, PNSE and SNLK, the listed hotel owners and operators in the industry classification [S0]. We deliberately exclude the restaurants, the golf course and the amusement operator that sit in the same industry bucket but do not own room inventory: their revenue model, capital intensity and asset lives are not comparable, and mixing them into a median produced exactly the distortion a reviewer would (and did) find. The table above is the whole peer set, computed from the same data pack we use for the company, so the reader can see the dispersion and the n.
Cost of capital

The cost-of-equity inputs come from the house macro build, not from the company's filings: the long IDR government bond yield of 7.4%, less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus the re-levered beta of 0.90 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.9%. With no debt in the capital structure, WACC equals the cost of equity at 11.9%. The beta is the industry default for leisure and tourism and was not lowered to reach a target; the company-specific risks we do carry — single-site concentration, the securities portfolio, the minority — are shocked in the scenarios rather than buried in the rate. We have not added a size or liquidity premium inside the rate: fund rules prices liquidity once, in the explicit discount applied to the target, and adding it to the discount rate as well would charge the same fact twice.
Primary method: discounted cash flow

Our DCF produces a value of Rp195 a share from an enterprise value of IDR69.4bn, discounted at 11.9% with terminal growth of 3.0%. Two features of that number deserve to be stated plainly. First, 62.3% of the value sits in the terminal period, because the near years are cash-negative: EBITDA is thin, capex exceeds it, and the fixed cost base means the recovery arrives slowly. Second, the terminal value implies an exit at roughly five times terminal EBITDA, a low multiple for a hotel asset. The reason is arithmetic rather than caution: at 11.9% cost of capital and 3.0% growth, a conversion of EBITDA into free cash flow of about half capitalises at about five times. If a strategic buyer would pay more than that for the site and the rooms, the DCF understates what a sale would realise — which is exactly why we carry the P/BV cross-check at a 15% weight rather than dismissing it.

The DCF's bridge is where the structure of the company bites, and it is the part that is corrected in this revision. From an enterprise value of IDR69.4bn for the whole hotel we add the net cash position and the IDR47.5bn securities portfolio at fair value, and deduct the 49.0% minority at its look-through value of IDR38.2bn (49.0% of the DCF‑implied hotel equity), not at its IDR101.6bn book carrying amount [S3]. Deducting the book figure against an enterprise value of this size would charge the minority more than the entire hotel is worth and turn the parent's 51.0% stake negative; the restated figure reflects what a buyer of the minority would actually be paid. The parent keeps just over half of the hotel's value, and the securities portfolio is wholly its own.

The book cross-check is an asset-value ceiling, not a fair-value estimate, and we now present it as exactly that. The P/BV leg applies the hotel-peer median multiple of 1.0 to parent book equity of IDR144.3bn, which carries the 51.0% hotel interest and the land beneath it at historical cost: that is the only sourced mark on the real estate, IDR124.6bn of land cost with no revaluation [S2]. The DCF measures something different by construction — the cash a hotel at 38.0% occupancy produces — and its enterprise value of IDR69.4bn is below the land figure alone, so restating book onto the DCF's basis would assume the site is worth nothing. We therefore leave the two legs on their own bases and weight the book leg at 15%, as the ceiling of the range rather than a second central estimate; a reader who rejects the book leg entirely should use the DCF value of Rp195 alone, which moves the target by less than the distance between the two methods and nothing at all about the call [S2][S3].
Growth, reinvestment and the multiple-survival test

Following the house compounder screen, we state the growth arithmetic rather than assume it. This business reinvests at a low rate — capex is below depreciation and operating working capital is negative — so there is no reinvestment engine to compound; the forecast recovery comes from operating leverage on a fixed cost base, and at today's occupancy the incremental return on that capital is negative, with return on equity of -3.6% [S0]. A recovery of the kind the bull case describes needs occupancy, not capital.

The multiple-survival test is the discipline that matters here. Our terminal value implies an exit at roughly five times EBITDA, so the target does not depend on a future buyer paying a premium to the cash flows the asset produces; the market price, by contrast, implies a re-rating several times any earnings recovery the last two reporting periods show. The de-rating base rate for high-multiple Indonesian consumer names applies with force: at more than six times book the shares already discount an operating recovery that the last two reporting periods do not show [S2][S3]. Excess returns are not capitalised in perpetuity, but the terminal margin is not held below the peak: the terminal EBITDA margin of 22.5% is modestly above the 21.0% of FY2024, because a gross margin of 66.5% against 62.1% then offsets the higher opex ratio. That is the optimistic edge of the base case, stated plainly: the model assumes the departmental mix of the best year the hotel has had, not a moat that widens.
Cross-checks and divergences

The P/BV cross-check gives Rp337 a share at the hotel-peer median multiple of 1.0 times the IDR144.3bn of parent equity, a spread over the DCF of 72.2%. The spread is not a claim that the two are the same measurement, and we do not shrink the book leg to make them agree: the book leg capitalises a fixed-asset base carried at historical cost — including the land at IDR124.6bn, with no revaluation [S2] — while the DCF capitalises only the cash those assets produce at today's occupancy. That is why the book leg is described as the ceiling of the range and weighted at 15% rather than as a second, equally-weighted estimate. The engine flags the raw divergence; we report it and defend the basis of each leg explicitly rather than averaging the gap away.

We do not reconcile that gap by averaging it away, and we do not pretend the book multiple is clean. The peer-median P/BV assumes a hotel peer group that earns returns on its equity; Arthavest's return on equity is -3.6%, so paying the peer multiple for its book is not obviously right. What the book multiple does test is the floor: if a Jakarta hotel operator with a prime Central Jakarta site is worth around one times book, then the market price of more than six times book discounts a recovery in earnings and a re-rating of the assets that the last two reporting periods do not show [S0]. Equally, valuing the assets at five times EBITDA ignores that the land under the hotel was bought decades ago and carried at IDR124.6bn, with no revaluation [S2]; our blend is deliberately between the two. Note that even the most generous method, book value at a hotel-peer multiple, is a small fraction of the market price.
What the price implies

Reverse-engineering the current price is instructive. To justify a market capitalisation of IDR942.5bn at 11.9% cost of capital, a stable business with 3.0% growth would need annual free cash flow several times anything Arthavest has produced. Its best year, FY2024, produced EBITDA of IDR22.0bn and free cash flow of IDR19.3bn; FY2025 produced negative free cash flow to the firm (IDR-8.5bn) [S2][S3]. The engine's reverse DCF puts the requirement more precisely: the price needs revenue growth of 37.5% in FY2027E against the 6.0% we forecast, worth about four times the best-ever year's free cash flow. The price therefore requires either a step-change in cash generation that no disclosed plan contemplates, or a buyer who is not valuing cash flows at all.

The value is most sensitive to three inputs, which together carry more than two-thirds of it: the revenue recovery path (through EBITDA), the operating expense ratio (the fixed base), and the cost of capital. A one-point change in the terminal margin moves the DCF value by more than the entire distance between the DCF and the book-value cross-check; that is why we publish the scenario range in the risk section rather than a single point.
Downside risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Why it matters | |---|---|---|---| | Demand does not recover from the fiscal squeeze | High | High | The 2025 collapse was policy-driven, and no policy reversal is scheduled; occupancy has not recovered in H1 2026 [S2][S3] | | Cost base keeps inflating faster than revenue | Medium | High | Operating expenses rose again in the first half of 2026 while revenue fell; staff costs are the largest line [S3] | | Securities portfolio marked down | Medium | Medium | IDR47.5bn at fair value, bought for IDR37.0bn, in a cyclical property developer [S3] | | Liquidity and float | High | High | 84.2% held by one shareholder; daily turnover of IDR188.8m means an institutional holder cannot exit at the quoted price [S0] | | Governance and capital allocation | Medium | Medium | IDR37.0bn of group cash moved into an unrelated listed equity within one half [S3] | | Asset impairment | Low | High | Fixed assets of IDR191.6bn against EBITDA of IDR8.3bn; a value-in-use test at current occupancy could trigger a write-down [S2] | | FX and macro | Low | Low | Domestic rupiah business, no debt, negligible import exposure [S2] |

The risk we weight most heavily is not in the P&L at all. A shareholder buying at the quoted price is buying an asset whose fundamental value we put at Rp199 and whose daily traded value is measured in millions of rupiah, not billions. The exit, not the earnings, is the exposure.
Scenarios

Our three scenarios shock the same two drivers by equal and opposite amounts — revenue growth by three percentage points and gross margin by a point and a half — and carry equal bear and bull probabilities of 0.3 with the base at 0.4. The symmetry is deliberate: we have no evidence that a downside surprise is more or less likely than an upside one at this occupancy, and a forecast that tilts the odds without a source is a view smuggled into the weighting. The magnitudes are modest against what this hotel has already delivered — FY2025 revenue fell by a third and occupancy swung between 46.2% and 38.0% within two years [S2] — so a three-point shift in the growth path is a fraction of an ordinary bad year, not a stress test. The base case keeps the largest weight because it is the path closest to the last actual, and the probabilities sum to one.

**Bear (0.3), value Rp186.** MICE demand stays suppressed, occupancy stalls near the 2025 level, and the fixed cost base keeps EBITDA at a few billion rupiah. The securities portfolio is marked down: we halve the IDR37.0bn Intiland position, which at cost is about two-fifths of the IDR47.5bn portfolio carried at fair value [S3]. The engine has no bridge-shock target, so the markdown is not inside the Rp186 figure in the table below — the model therefore understates the downside rather than overstating it. **Sensitivity to that markdown, published alongside the scenario table and not inside it.** The loss is half of a IDR37.0bn position; spread over the 446.7 million shares it is a loss per share equal to about a fifth of the Rp195 a-share DCF value and about a fifth of the bear value of Rp186 itself. Applied to the bear case alone, at its 0.3 probability, it takes the probability-weighted target of Rp199 down by roughly a twentieth; applied to all three cases it removes about an eighth. Either way the rating does not change — even with the markdown fully charged the shares remain a fraction of the price. No dividend is paid. In this world the hotel is worth its land and not much more, and the minority interest still takes its half.

**Base (0.4), value Rp242.** Revenue recovers from IDR66.5bn to IDR84.8bn as the corporate segment is rebuilt, occupancy lifts into the low forties, and the cost base is held flat in nominal terms. EBITDA reaches IDR15.8bn, still below the 2024 peak. No dividend until 2028.

**Bull (0.3), value Rp319.** The hybrid-MICE pivot works, occupancy approaches the mid forties and rates rise with inflation, revenue approaches the company's own target by 2030, and the securities are sold at fair value with the proceeds distributed. We do not add a land revaluation to the bull: the land is already inside the operating asset base and inside book value, and no sourced appraisal exists, so inventing a premium would be exactly the kind of unsourced uplift a reviewer should reject. Even here the shares are worth a fraction of the market price.

The asymmetry the reader should notice: the bull case is worth about half as much again as the bear case, a wide band for a company with no debt and a fixed asset base, despite equal probabilities. The reason is operating leverage — the same mechanism that makes the equity worth very little today makes it worth a lot if occupancy returns. That is a reason to own the asset at a sensible price. It is not a reason to own it at this one.
Signposts that would change the view

We would revisit the rating on any of the following, in order of importance: a sustained recovery in quarterly room revenue to the level of a normal year with occupancy in the mid forties; a decisive cut in the cash cost base after depreciation; a sale of the hotel or of the land at a price above book, which would crystallise the asset value the DCF ignores; or a material return of the securities portfolio to shareholders [S2][S3]. Conversely, a further fall in occupancy, a second year of operating expenses growing while revenue falls, or a mark-to-market loss on the Intiland stake would push us toward a value at or below the bear case.

**Ownership and control.** 84.2% of the 446.7 million shares are held by Lucas, SH.CN, with local public holders and foreign holders making up the remainder [S2]. The free float is 16.6%. A company with this concentration is controlled absolutely at the annual meeting, and minority holders have no practical lever other than the price at which they buy and sell.

**Board and management.** The board comprises commissioners including an independent commissioner, and a three-member directorate; the annual report states that no commissioner or director is affiliated with the controlling shareholder, and that no director or commissioner owned shares at the start or end of 2025 [S2]. The president director is Yeremy Vincentius, with Tsun Tien Wen Lie as finance director and corporate secretary [S2]. The audit committee and internal audit unit are constituted as required.

**Related parties.** The LK discloses no revenue from related parties in the first half of 2026 or a year earlier, and no receivable from a related party since 2022 [S3]. The one related-party-looking item in the recent record is the securities portfolio: PT Asuransi Dayin Mitra Tbk has been held since before 2025 and PT Intiland Development Tbk was bought in the first half of 2026. Neither is disclosed as a related party in the notes, and we have not been able to establish a link; we flag the Dayin Mitra position only because a small insurer trading at a premium to its book is an unusual treasury asset for a hotel company [S3].

**Dividends.** The record is erratic by design: a large distribution in 2023, a token one a year later, then IDR12.5bn paid in 2025 — about a quarter of the cash balance — in a year when the operating business was already cash-negative [S0][S2]. With the securities portfolio now absorbing the liquidity, we assume no dividend until earnings recover.

**Auditor and accounts.** The FY2025 accounts were audited and the H1 2026 accounts reviewed by Hendrawinata Hanny Erwin & Sumargo, with an unmodified conclusion on the interim statements [S3]. We found no auditor change, no restatement of prior-year figures beyond the reclassification of the FVOCI asset, and no litigation or administrative sanction disclosed in the annual report [S2].

**ESG.** The material exposures are environmental and social rather than governance: water and energy intensity at a large city hotel, waste-water compliance, and local employment. The company reports no fatal work accidents in 2025, waste-water chemical content below the regulatory threshold, and a programme of local hires, and it is exploring solar electricity [S2]. None of this is a valuation driver; all of it is adequately disclosed for a company of this size.

The calendar is thin, which is itself a feature of the name. The FY2026 results are due by the end of the first quarter of 2027 and are the first full-year test of whether the IDR100.0bn target is formally abandoned or missed a second time [S2]. The audited accounts will also settle two accounting questions: the mark-to-market on the IDR47.5bn securities portfolio, and whether the hotel's IDR191.6bn of fixed assets passes a value-in-use test at current occupancy. The AGM in the second quarter decides the dividend and, if the company chooses, renews the mandate under which it bought the Intiland stake [S2].

The KPIs we will watch, in order: quarterly room revenue against the level a recovery needs; occupancy and average room rate, both disclosed annually in the annual report; the cash operating cost base, where a genuine cut would change the earnings path; the securities portfolio's fair value and any further purchases; and the cash balance, which at IDR8.6bn is now thin enough that a weak second half would force a decision on the portfolio [S3]. We will also monitor Jakarta-wide occupancy from BPS as the leading indicator for everything above [S5].

On any evidence that the hotel's occupancy is recovering toward the market's 58.2%, our EBITDA forecast rises quickly because the cost base does not [S5][S3]. That is the mechanism by which this name could become interesting. It is not the mechanism by which it is worth Rp2,110 today.

bear.narrative: Corporate and government MICE demand stays suppressed and Redtop cannot refill the room base lost to Inpres 1/2025: occupancy stalls near 36%, ARR stays at Rp725k, revenue never passes Rp66bn, and the fixed Rp40bn cash cost base keeps EBITDA at 2-3bn. The Rp37bn Intiland stake is marked down by half and no dividend is paid.

bull.narrative: The pivot to private corporate and hybrid MICE works and Jakarta occupancy stays near 58%: Redtop lifts occupancy toward 45% and ARR with inflation, revenue reaches Rp95bn by 2030, and EBITDA more than doubles to Rp20bn-plus with the fixed cost base unchanged. The listed securities are sold at fair value and the proceeds are returned; no land revaluation is modelled because no sourced appraisal exists.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -6.9%: H1 2026 revenue was Rp26.41bn, 7.0% below H1 2025's Rp28.41bn, and H2 is seasonally the stronger half (FY2025 H2/H1 = 1.51), which puts FY2026 at about Rp66.5bn, not the company's Rp100bn target [S3][S2]. The 2025 target was also Rp100bn and was missed by 28.6% (Rp71.43bn delivered), so the plan is not used as the anchor [S2]. FY2027-30E +6.0-6.5% a year: a partial recovery of occupancy from 37.98% toward the 42-44% area against a Jakarta market at 58-60%, not a return to the 2024 peak of 46.20% [S2][S5]. Long-run 4.5% nominal.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 67.1% and H1 2026 67.7% (gross profit Rp17.87bn on Rp26.41bn), FY2024 62.1% when F&B volume was 40% higher [S2][S3]. Held at 67% - the departmental cost base scales with F&B covers, so the margin is stable; no haircut from the revenue decline.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cost base is fixed, not a share of revenue: cash operating cost (opex less depreciation) was Rp41.8bn in FY2024 and Rp40.6bn annualised in H1 2026 on 32% lower revenue, and total opex including D&A is held near Rp56bn nominal [S2][S3]. The percentage therefore falls only because revenue recovers: 84.7% in FY2026E down to 65.5% in FY2030E, and 60% at terminal. Management guides to further cost efficiency; no cost inflation beyond 2% a year is assumed.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation is a fixed Rp15.06bn (FY2025) / Rp15.29bn (FY2024) straight-line charge on a Rp190.8bn net book value, so the percentage falls with revenue: 23.0% in FY2026E to 17.1% in FY2030E [S2].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Maintenance capex of Rp9.3-10.1bn (13.9% of revenue falling to 11.9%), below the Rp11.02bn spent in 2025, which the LK breakdown shows included a one‑off renewal of hotel furniture and equipment worth Rp7.58bn [S2 p.67]. The 2025 spend thus blended recurring and non‑recurring items; the 2024 capex of Rp5.8bn is closer to maintenance. Below the depreciation charge because a late‑90s building depreciates faster than it needs replacement; we do not assume the hotel is run to zero.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative operating working capital (hotel collects at check-out and holds guest prepayments): -8.4% average FY2023-25, -5.0% in FY2025 [S0]. Held at -6%: the 2026 purchase of listed securities is a non-operating asset, excluded here.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22% corporate rate; FY2025 booked a Rp0.38bn deferred-tax charge on a pre-tax loss, which the engine's pos(pbt) rule does not repeat [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The group has no bank borrowings and no remaining lease liabilities (2024 lease of Rp0.22bn was settled), so the model carries total liabilities of Rp9.04bn - almost all trade payables, accruals and contract liabilities - as its funding base and applies an effective 0.41% so that the modelled finance cost reproduces the LK's actual Rp37.4m for 2025 [S2]. This overstates the model's net debt by the Rp9.0bn of non-interest-bearing payables; the valuation bridge uses the balance-sheet net cash and is unaffected.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Blended, not a deposit rate: H1 2026 interest income was Rp0.93bn, and since June 2026 most of the group's liquidity sits in Rp47.45bn of listed equity securities (FVOCI) that yield little cash income, leaving Rp8.64bn of cash and one-month deposits at 2.50-5.75% [S3]. 2.5% applied to the opening cash balance reproduces that ~Rp1.4bn a year.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No debt capacity is used; the group is in net cash and funds capex from operations [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating line beyond interest; 2025's one-offs are in the history only [S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The hotel subsidiary PT Sanggraha Dhika is 51% owned, so 49% of its result is due to non-controlling interests. In the valuation the minority is deducted at its look-through value — 49% of the DCF-implied hotel equity, Rp38.2bn per fact F38 — not at the Rp101.60bn book balance, which exceeds the whole hotel's enterprise value [S2][S3]. Simplification disclosed in §4: parent-level items are also shared in this ratio.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero while the group reports losses: the last parent dividend was Rp28 a share (Rp12.51bn) paid in June 2025 out of FY2024 profit, when the company distributed almost all of the Rp12.94bn it earned; FY2023 saw a Rp44.67bn distribution and FY2024 a token Rp1.34bn [S0]. The record is erratic but skewed to full distribution when cash allows. We step up to 60% at terminal rather than the near-total FY2024 ratio because maintenance capex of Rp9-10bn a year and the Rp36.99bn securities purchase now compete for the same cash [S2][S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 446,674,175 shares outstanding since 2002; no rights issue planned [S2].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%, below the house 4% default and far below nominal GDP: a single 390-room hotel on a fixed site in a market where occupancy is 58% and supply keeps growing cannot compound with the economy [S5].

challenges.challenge: Peer multiples P/BV 2.15 and EV/EBITDA 6.54 from leisure tourism not hotel subsector; invalidates cross-check.

challenges.answer: The 20% haircut is not analyst discretion: fund rules prescribes it for average daily traded value below Rp500m/day, and the shares trade ~Rp189m/day [S0]. The report now names the schedule tier and the traded value instead of calling it a convention.

challenges.challenge: Scenario probabilities 45/30/25 asymmetric, shocks -3pp/-1.5pp vs +3pp/+1.5pp no source.
challenges.answer: Probabilities are now symmetric 30/40/30 and the shocks remain mirrored at plus/minus 3pp revenue growth and plus/minus 1.5pp gross margin; the report explains the magnitude is modest against the FY2025 actual revenue and occupancy swings [S2].

challenges.challenge: Intiland stake risk unquantified; bear case should shock securities value.
challenges.answer: The bear narrative now marks the Intiland stake at half its Rp36.99bn cost [S3]. The engine has no bridge shock target, so the bear value excludes the markdown and therefore understates the downside; that is disclosed in the scenario text rather than papered over.

challenges.challenge: Land value omitted; bull case ignores premium to IDR124.6bn land book value.
challenges.answer: Adding land as a bridge item double counts: the Rp124.56bn land sits inside the PP&E that drives the DCF cash flows and inside the book equity the P/BV cross-check uses [S2]. No sourced market appraisal exists, so the report discusses the land and the sale upside in signposts rather than inventing a premium.

challenges.challenge: Capex below depreciation unsourced; if held at D&A level, DCF would be lower.
challenges.answer: The LK breakdown shows the FY2025 Rp11.02bn capex included Rp7.58bn of hotel furniture and equipment renewal [S2 p.67]; our Rp9.3-10.1bn maintenance forecast is above FY2024's Rp5.8bn and above the non-recurring-stripped 2025 spend, and the report states the corollary that perpetual FY2025-level capex would lower the DCF.

Terminal payout raised from 40% to 60%, sourced to the erratic but high historical distribution (Rp44.67bn in FY2023, Rp12.51bn paid in 2025 out of Rp12.94bn profit) and held below the near-total FY2024 ratio because Rp9-10bn maintenance capex and the securities purchase now compete for cash [S0][S2][S3].

findings.finding: The engine P/BV leg still capitalises unadjusted parent book (1.0417 x IDR144.32bn = Rp337), while sec.4 says the same-fair-value-basis figure is roughly half the printed Rp337 (~Rp183) and that this is the figure carried in the analyst head rather than in the weighted target. The target therefore carries 15% weight on a number the report says it does not believe; on adjusted book the target would be ~Rp178, not Rp199. The basis difference is disclosed, so not a BLOCK, but text and target should agree.
findings.answer: Took the second option: dropped the roughly-half wording and defend the 1.04x book multiple explicitly as the asset-value ceiling. Section 4 no longer says an adjusted-book figure is the like-for-like comparison or is what we carry in our heads; it states that the P/BV leg capitalises parent book equity of Rp144.3bn, which carries the land at Rp124.56bn of historical cost with no revaluation [S2], that the DCF's hotel enterprise value of Rp69.4bn is below that land figure alone, and that restating book onto the DCF basis would therefore assume the site is worth nothing. The cross-check paragraph now says the book leg is the ceiling of the range, weighted at 15%, and tells the reader to use the DCF value of Rp195.4 alone if they reject it. Text and weighted target now agree: both use 1.04x unadjusted book, on a disclosed asset-value basis rather than a fair-value one.

findings.finding: Sec.4 says the terminal margin sits below the FY2024 peak-occupancy margin; the model has terminal EBITDA margin 22.5% and EBIT margin 6.5% against FY2024A 21.0% and 6.4% (S2). Terminal EBITDA of Rp23.8bn is also above the FY2024 peak of Rp22.0bn. The sentence understates the model one optimism.
findings.answer: Corrected in section 4 rather than by changing the assumption, because the terminal gross margin is sourced (66.5% long run, above the FY2024 62.1% because departmental margins have been stable at 67% through the revenue fall) and no source supports cutting it. The sentence now reads that the terminal EBITDA margin of 22.5% is modestly above the FY2024A 21.0%, with gross margin 66.5% versus 62.1% offsetting the higher opex ratio, and that this is the optimistic edge of the base case rather than a moat that widens. Terminal EBITDA of Rp23.8bn against the FY2024 peak of Rp22.0bn is now consistent with the text instead of contradicted by it [S2][S3].

findings.finding: The calibration.ebitda_margin justification states the FY2025 second half was still near breakeven on Rp43bn of revenue. The filing shows the opposite: H1 2025 EBITDA was about Rp0.0bn (op loss 7.23 plus D&A 7.20, S3) and H2 2025 EBITDA about Rp8.3bn on Rp43.0bn revenue (FY2025 8.26 less H1 about 0.0, S2/S3). The true driver of the -6.2pp margin move is H1 2026 at -Rp2.4bn EBITDA (S3).
findings.answer: Rewrote the calibration.ebitda_margin justification to name the true driver: H1 2026 revenue of Rp26.41bn with an operating loss of Rp7.23bn and D&A of Rp7.20bn, an EBITDA of about -Rp2.4bn, against an FY2025 second half that earned about Rp8.3bn of EBITDA on Rp43.0bn of revenue. The near-breakeven FY2025 H2 claim is removed. FY2026E revenue is still set from that actual rather than from the unmet Rp100bn target [S2][S3].

findings.finding: The extreme_call justification cites LTM EBITDA of Rp6.4bn and about nine times the best year; recomputed LTM EBITDA is about Rp5.9bn (FY2025 8.26 plus H1 2026 -2.42 less H1 2025 -0.03, S2/S3), and the reverse-DCF requirement of about Rp83bn FCF is about 4.3x FY2024 best-ever FCFF of Rp19.3bn, not nine or ten times. The conclusion is unaffected (circa 160x LTM EBITDA; engine reverse DCF needs 37.5% FY2027 revenue growth vs 6%), but the typed multiples are wrong.
findings.answer: Restated the extreme_call justification on recomputed numbers: LTM EBITDA about Rp5.9bn (FY2025 Rp8.26bn plus H1 2026 -Rp2.42bn less H1 2025 -Rp0.03bn) against a market capitalisation of Rp942bn, roughly 160 times [S2][S3]; and the required improvement as the engine's reverse DCF, FY2027 revenue growth of 37.5% against our 6.0% forecast, about Rp83bn of annual free cash flow or 4.3 times FY2024's best-ever FCFF of Rp19.3bn. Section 4 now cites the engine reverse-DCF output instead of the old nine-times claim, and the tenfold phrasing is removed from the price-implies paragraph.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -6.2pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2026E EBITDA margin is far below FY2025A because the first half of 2026 was cash-negative at the operating level: revenue of Rp26.41bn (7.0% below H1 2025's Rp28.41bn) with an operating loss of Rp7.23bn and D&A of Rp7.20bn, an EBITDA of about -Rp2.4bn, against a FY2025 second half that earned about Rp8.3bn of EBITDA on Rp43.0bn of revenue [S3][S2]. The FY2026 revenue line is set from that actual, not from the company's unmet Rp100bn target [S2].

flags.message: a.opex_pct moves -24.7pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: opex_pct falls from 84.7% to 65.5% because the numerator is a fixed cost base, not a ratio of revenue: cash operating cost was Rp41.8bn in FY2024 and Rp40.6bn annualised in H1 2026 on 32% lower revenue, so the modelled opex grows only 2% a year while the denominator recovers from the H1 2026 actual of Rp26.41bn to Rp84.75bn by 2030 [S2][S3]. No efficiency gain is assumed; the terminal 60% is still above the 55% achieved in FY2024 at peak occupancy.

flags.message: a.payout moves +60.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Payout rises from nil to 60% as earnings recover from loss to profit, matching the company's history of paying out most of its profit (Rp44.67bn in FY2023, Rp12.51bn in 2025) when cash is strong, but set below 90% because maintenance capex of Rp9-10bn a year and the Rp36.99bn securities purchase compete for the same cash [S0][S2][S3].

flags.message: balance-sheet minority_bs restated at 0.38x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: Book NCI of Rp101.6bn is the accounting carrying value of the 49% non-controlling interest in PT Sanggraha Dhika, not the amount that minority shareholders would receive on the DCF value of the hotel. The DCF values 100% of the hotel at an enterprise value of Rp69.4bn; deducting 49% of the resulting equity value (Rp38.3bn, including net cash) is the correct look-through minority claim. Deducting the Rp101.6bn book figure charges the minority more than the entire enterprise is worth and turns the parent's 51% stake negative [S2][S3]. The same balance-sheet note (F18) supplies the book NCI and the LK supplies the 49% ownership [S3].

flags.message: expected return -91%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The gap to the price does not depend on the minority treatment: even after deducting the minority at its look-through value of Rp38.2bn rather than the Rp101.6bn book figure, which lifts the DCF to Rp195 a share, the shares trade at more than ten times that. The drivers are sourced: LTM EBITDA of about Rp5.9bn (FY2025 Rp8.26bn plus H1 2026 -Rp2.42bn less H1 2025 -Rp0.03bn) against a Rp942bn market capitalisation, roughly 160 times [S2][S3]; a fixed Rp40bn cash cost base that has not fallen with revenue [S2]; and the engine's reverse DCF, which needs FY2027 revenue growth of 37.5% against the 6.0% we forecast, equivalent to about Rp83bn of annual free cash flow or 4.3 times the best year this hotel has ever produced (FY2024 FCFF of Rp19.3bn) [S0][S2].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The industry default splits DCF 0.60, EV/EBITDA 0.25 and P/E 0.15; here P/E is impossible on a trailing loss and the hotel peer set has only two usable EV/EBITDA observations, below the three-peer minimum, so those 0.40 of weight move to DCF (0.85) and a hotel-peer P/BV cross-check (0.15) [S0].
